title: Checkpoint: Learning and Habits
objective: After this level you can explain how association, consequences and watching others shape what we do.
summary: Learning is a lasting change from experience. Signals teach through classical conditioning, consequences through operant conditioning, and models through observation.

cards.headline: Chapter 3 finale: three ways experience rewires what you do.
cards.body: A dog drools at a tone. A rat presses a lever for food. A child copies an adult hitting a doll. Each one learned something, by a different route. First, what counts as learning; then the three routes side by side.

cards.headline: What counts as learning
cards.body: Psychologists define learning as a relatively permanent change in behavior or knowledge that results from experience. Most of this chapter was associative learning: making connections between things that happen together, like a tone and food, or a lever and a pellet. Classical and operant conditioning both need direct experience. Observational learning stretches the reach, because you can learn by watching others.

items.label: Classical (Pavlov)
points: Learn that one stimulus predicts another
The stimulus comes just before the response

items.label: Operant (Skinner)
points: Learn that a behavior brings a consequence
The consequence comes after the behavior

items.label: Observational (Bandura)
points: Rewards shape doing more than learning

cards.headline: Lessons that stick
cards.body: Across the chapter, learning proved hard to undo. Extinction lays a new lesson over an old one instead of erasing it. Unpredictable rewards keep a behavior going longest. Repetition in one setting ties a response to its cues until it runs on its own. And a caution: the famous Little Albert result rested on a single infant.

cards.headline: Chapter 3 complete
learned: How a signal, a consequence or a model can each teach a new behavior.
Why an extinguished response can return, and what that says about unlearning.
Why unpredictable rewards, like a slot machine's, keep a behavior going longest.

options.label: A relatively permanent change from experience
Any reflex an animal is born with
A change in behavior produced only by rewards
options.rationale: Classical and observational learning need no reward.

options.rationale: Learning covers behavior as well as knowledge.

questions.explanation: Learning is a relatively permanent change in behavior or knowledge that results from experience.

questions.prompt: Match each route to learning with how it works.
questions.explanation: In classical conditioning you learn that one stimulus predicts another. In operant conditioning you learn that a behavior brings a consequence. In observational learning you learn by watching a model.

questions.prompt: Why can an extinguished response come back?

options.label: The conditioned stimulus became much louder
The animal was rewarded again
options.rationale: The response returns without any new reward.

options.label: The response was a reflex all along
options.rationale: It was learned, which is why it could fade.

options.label: Extinction added new learning, not erasure

questions.explanation: Extinction lays new, context-dependent learning over the original, which is still there.

questions.prompt: In Garcia and Koelling's study, what made rats avoid a flavor?

options.label: Foot shocks after drinking
options.rationale: Shocked rats avoided the lights and sounds instead.

options.label: Watching other rats drink
options.rationale: The rats learned from their own experience.

questions.explanation: Rats made ill after the flavored water learned to avoid its taste.

questions.prompt: Most gambling pays out on a _____ schedule.

options.label: fixed interval
options.rationale: That's predictable timing, the easiest to extinguish.

options.label: fixed ratio
options.rationale: Slot machines don't pay after a set count.

questions.explanation: Most gambling pays after an unpredictable number of plays, a variable ratio schedule.
